idiom_name: public interface plus package-private implementation class, wired by a factory
implementation_notes: Java's binary compatibility rules already perform the pimpl job, so the local realization is the interface/implementation split rather than a pointer wrapper: deleting or changing private fields, methods and constructors is binary compatible, and adding fields or methods to a class does not break pre-existing binaries, because clients link by name against class files instead of re-reading a header (JLS chapter 13). The idiom is a public interface or abstract class as the contract, package-private implementation classes in the same package (or in a package that a JPMS module does not export), and a static factory or DI binding that hands out the contract. A hand-written forwarding wrapper would add an indirection per method to buy a firewall the platform already provides, so reserve it for wrapping a native handle that must stay behind a stable object.
pitfalls: Private implementation is safe to change, but the contract is not: removing a public or protected member, or narrowing its access, throws NoSuchMethodError or IllegalAccessError in already-compiled clients.

Package-private is invisible on the class declaration, so a refactor that splits or renames the package silently promotes the implementation into other packages' compile-time view - and packages are not hierarchical, so moving one level deeper in the tree loses access entirely.

Reflection-based frameworks can call setAccessible and reach private members anyway, so this is an encapsulation discipline, not a security boundary; JPMS exports is the stronger, module-level version.
